item.content: {"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=long-term+stability+and+preference+drift+in+reinforcement+learning+from+human+feedback+models&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"From Artificial to Embodied and Physical Intelligence in Smart Manufacturing.\", \"abstract\": \"Manufacturing is evolving from automation-centered production toward systems capable of sensing, adaptation, and autonomous response across digital, mechanical, and material domains. Although recent progress has been largely driven by artificial intelligence, current manufacturing intelligence often remains external to physical systems and suffers from limited robustness, interpretability, and transferability in complex industrial environments. Here, we present a unified perspective on smart manufacturing through the framework of artificial intelligence (AI), embodied intelligence (EI), and physical intelligence (PI). AI provides abstraction, prediction, and generative capability; EI enables closed-loop perception, decision-making, and physical interaction; and PI embeds adaptive intelligence directly into materials, structures, and physicochemical processes. We further discuss how generative intelligence is beginning to connect these domains through inverse design, adaptive fabrication, and physics-constrained behavior realization. Recent advances in collaborative robotics, embodied digital twins, self-optimizing production systems, and physically intelligent materials, including self-actuating, self-healing, multistable, and shape-morphing systems, are reviewed. Finally, we propose an integrated AI-EI-PI framework spanning the full manufacturing lifecycle, highlighting a transition toward manufacturing systems in which intelligence is increasingly co-designed across algorithms, embodied agents, and matter itself.\", \"doi\": \"10.1002/advs.78384\", \"pmid\": \"42932218\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13703982\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.78384\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \…

models, and challenges.\", \"abstract\": \"Search and Rescue (SAR) robotics increasingly depends on collaborative intelligence to operate effectively in dynamic, uncertain, and time-sensitive environments. Modern SAR missions require coordinated interaction among heterogeneous robotic agents as well as structured collaboration between humans and intelligent systems for perception, decision-making, and adaptive mission execution. This paper presents a structured narrative review supported by a systematic literature search of learning-enabled collaborative intelligence frameworks in SAR robotics, organized around three paradigms: human-to-machine (H2M), machine-to-machine (M2M), and machine-to-human (M2H) learning. The review examines recent developments in reinforcement learning, federated and decentralized learning, knowledge distillation, swarm intelligence, semantic communication, and the growing integration of large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) for knowledge grounding, transfer, and explainability. Beyond algorithmic advances, the analysis emphasizes deployment-oriented challenges including partial observability, communication constraints, uncertainty management, model reliability, and real-time operational requirements. Rather than conducting a fully PRISMA-compliant systematic review, this work synthesizes representative and influential studies to identify emerging trends, architectural trade-offs, deployment limitations, and future research directions for scalable and trustworthy collaborative SAR systems.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/frobt.2026.1832982\", \"pmid\": \"42952483\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13713275\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2026.1832982\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13713275\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13713275?pdf=render\"}]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "08210a8e7615cc47a3cbedf3f3e034d6a5fce522333546a2635a8cfdd0c6b54c", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "emergent_preferences", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.1002/advs.78384", "doi:10.3389/frobt.2026.1832982", "pmc:PMC13703982", "pmc:PMC13667652", "pmc:PMC13657930", "pmc:PMC13713275"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.78384", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13703982", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13703982?pdf=render", "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13667652/?tool=EBI", "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13667652/pdf/?tool=EBI", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13667652", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13667652?pdf=render", "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13657930/?tool=EBI"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
